# Incident Report — MTA-2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Evidence Reviewed
- `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB, capture window 2026-01-28 03:04:03 → 03:14:27 +0400, ~624 sec). No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence folder — analysis is based entirely on the pcap via tshark.

## Victim Host
| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.21.58** |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (confirmed via DHCP Option 12 and NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` registrations) |
| AD domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (NetBIOS `WIN11OFFICE`), DC = WIN-LU4L24X3UB7 at 10.1.21.2 |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString to realm WIN11OFFICE.COM) |

Note: normal AD background traffic (LDAP/CLDAP, Kerberos, SAMR, LSARPC, DRSUAPI DRSBind/DRSUnbind/DRSCrackNames — opnums 0, 1, 12 only, never DsGetNCChanges) was reviewed and is consistent with routine domain-joined workstation/GPO activity, not a DCSync or credential-dumping attempt.

## Malware Family
**Name:** SecTopRAT (aka ArechClient2)
**Attribution confidence: BEHAVIORAL, not signature-confirmed.** No AV/YARA hit or file hash on the actual dropped binary was possible — the payload was delivered over TLS with Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), so its filename, executable content, and hash are not recoverable from the capture. The call is based on distinctive network behavior:
- Delivery via a fake file-download portal chain (typosquat-style redirect → landing page → archive host).
- Post-execution phase in which the malware drives a Chromium-based browser engine to enumerate each installed browser individually (observed for both **Chrome** and **Edge**) and fingerprints it (WebGL/canvas/WebRTC/AudioContext/hardware), then reports the fingerprint back to the C2 as a "log" — the per-browser `agent=Chrome` / `agent=Edge` enumeration pattern is the specific TTP associated with this family's browser-data theft component, rather than generic anti-bot gating (the requests fire ~45–60 seconds *after* the archive download finishes, i.e. after execution, not during page browsing).

## Attack Timeline (relative to capture start)
1. **t≈45.3s** — Client resolves `hiyter.com` → 104.21.22.231/172.67.207.145 (redirector).
2. **t≈45.8s** — Resolves `media.megafilehub4.lat` → 104.21.48.156/172.67.154.67 (fake download landing page; loads `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `static.cloudflareinsights.com`).
3. **t≈48.3s** — Resolves `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` → 104.21.46.67/172.67.136.13. A 22-second, ~16 MB TLS/ECH download follows immediately (stream 10.1.21.58:54840 ↔ 104.21.46.67:443) — the malicious archive/dropper. Content is TLS-encrypted; filename/hash not recoverable.
4. **t≈90.5s** — First contact to `whooptm.cyou` (62.72.32.156:443) — post-execution C2 beacon.
5. **t≈92.5–107s** — Repeated contact to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49), both port 80 (plaintext, fully observed) and port 443. Plaintext HTTP reveals the C2 protocol:
   - `GET /api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome` → server returns an HTML page with embedded JS that fingerprints the browser (navigator, screen, WebGL, canvas, WebRTC, AudioContext) and POSTs the results to the same endpoint with `&act=log`.
   - Sequence repeats with `agent=Edge` ~7 seconds later — consistent with the malware iterating over each installed browser.
6. **t≈123.0s** — Contact to `holiday-forever.cc` (80.97.160.24:443).
7. **t≈126.6s** — Contact to `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (104.21.9.36:443).

## Indicators of Compromise

**C2 / malicious endpoints (IP:port):**
- 153.92.1.49:80 and :443 — `whitepepper.su` (primary C2/fingerprint-exfil panel)
- 62.72.32.156:443 — `whooptm.cyou`
- 80.97.160.24:443 — `holiday-forever.cc`
- 104.21.9.36:443 / 172.67.141.109:443 — `communicationfirewall-security.cc`

**Malicious domains:**
- whitepepper[.]su
- whooptm[.]cyou
- holiday-forever[.]cc
- communicationfirewall-security[.]cc
- filemegahab4[.]sbs (subdomain: arch.filemegahab4.sbs — archive/dropper host, 104.21.46.67 / 172.67.136.13)
- megafilehub4[.]lat (subdomain: media.megafilehub4.lat — landing page, 104.21.48.156 / 172.67.154.67)
- hiyter[.]com (initial redirector, 104.21.22.231 / 172.67.207.145)

**Malicious/C2 URLs observed in plaintext:**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST, exfils fingerprint)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST, exfils fingerprint)

**Bot/session identifiers:** id = `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`; token = `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`

**Transferred files / hashes:**
- The primary dropped payload (~16 MB, downloaded from arch.filemegahab4.sbs, stream port 54840) was transferred over TLS 1.3 with Encrypted Client Hello — its filename and SHA256 **cannot be recovered from this capture**.
- HTTP objects recovered in plaintext from the C2 (fingerprinting/telemetry pages, not the malware binary itself):
  - `set_agent?...agent=Chrome` (fingerprint-collector HTML/JS) — SHA256: `a1ee2e3055dc4ce0d60eb6c2c8a655e705b3607bd33d65794e67adf22a2a0124`
  - `set_agent?...agent=Edge` (fingerprint-collector HTML/JS) — SHA256: `8f97a4018d4b0675b9592660394cf5b73f1be2252e27aff64a8f160af9079f46`

## Summary
Host DESKTOP-ES9F3ML (10.1.21.58, MAC 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2), logged on as domain user `gwyatt`, was infected after browsing through a fake software/file-download chain (hiyter.com → media.megafilehub4.lat → arch.filemegahab4.sbs) that delivered an encrypted ~16 MB payload. Roughly 40–60 seconds after the download, the host began beaconing to four external domains, with full plaintext capture of a browser-fingerprinting/exfiltration cycle against each installed browser (Chrome, then Edge) to `whitepepper.su`. This behavior is consistent with SecTopRAT/ArechClient2; this is a behavioral call, not a signature/hash-confirmed identification, since the dropped binary itself was never observed in plaintext.
